title: Blessed are they whose sins are covered (Psalm 31 [32])
hookLine: one of seven penitential psalms; silence made the bones grow old

cards: A dent in someone's car, backed into in a parking lot, and nobody saw. A small lie to a friend. Something broken, said or taken, and never mentioned.
At first it's fine. Then it isn't. It sits in the stomach.

Whoever is carrying it gets short with people for no reason, avoids a certain face in the hallway, sleeps badly. Nothing outside has changed, but the weight grows. A psalm describes that weight, and what lifted it.

teach.h: BLESSED ARE THEY WHOSE SINS ARE COVERED.
teach.b: Psalm 31 in the Douay, 32 in most Bibles, starts at the end of the story, with the relief: "Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered." Then it goes back to tell how it got there.
"Because I was silent my bones grew old; whilst I cried out all the day long." Silent about the sin, groaning about everything else. Day and night, it says, thy hand was heavy upon me.
The Hebrew adds that the speaker's strength dried up as in summer heat. That's what the silence cost.
Then the turn: "I said I will confess against myself my injustice to the Lord: and thou hast forgiven the wickedness of my sin." How fast it happens: I said I will, and it's done.
The heaviness was never in the confessing. It was in the not confessing.
This is one of seven psalms the Church has long grouped as the penitential psalms, psalms of sorrow for sin; in the Douay they're 6, 31, 37, 50, 101, 129 and 142.
Cassiodorus, a sixth-century scholar, wrote about them as a set, and they became a standard devotion in Lent and in old prayer books.
Augustine's friend and biographer, Possidius, wrote that as Augustine lay dying, he had these psalms copied and put up on the wall by his bed, and read them, weeping.
Saint Paul quotes the opening lines too, to say forgiveness is a gift. Catholic readers often hear in it the logic of confession: say it out loud, and the weight lifts.

how: Catholics have long prayed the seven penitential psalms together, especially during Lent and as preparation for confession; Psalm 31 [32] is also read at Mass and in the Liturgy of the Hours.

games.q: you've done something wrong and told no one. you feel worn out and short with everyone. what does the psalmist finally do?
o: say, I will confess my injustice to the Lord.
games.why: I said I will confess against myself my injustice to the Lord: and thou hast forgiven. the turn happens almost at once.

practice: Find one small, recent wrong, not the biggest thing in your life: a sharp word, a shortcut, a bit of unkindness, and feel how much it weighs. If you pray, say it plainly to God in a sentence, the way the psalm does: I did this.
If you don't, say it plainly to yourself, without excuses, and notice honestly whether anything got lighter.

wordCard.voice: Penitential psalms. Seven psalms of sorrow for sin that the Church has prayed together for centuries, this one among them. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: blessed are they whose, the psalm's first words in the Vulgate.

carryVoice: Your line: silence was heavier. The psalm opens with the relief, not the weight. One hundred sixty-seven days, and counting.
